title: The Tyranny of the Average User
text:
In the late 1940s the American air force faced an embarrassing problem: pilots were crashing planes that were technically in perfect condition. Cockpits had been designed around the average pilot, measured across thousands of men in the previous decade.

A young researcher decided to check how many pilots actually matched that average across ten key dimensions. Out of more than four thousand, the answer was zero. Not a single pilot was average on all ten measures, and fewer than four percent were average on even three of them.

The conclusion was uncomfortable but productive. If nobody is average, a cockpit built for the average fits nobody. The solution was adjustability: movable seats, adjustable pedals, straps that could be changed in seconds. Today we take those things for granted in cars and offices, rarely noticing that they came from a statistical mistake with a body count.

title: Why Bureaucracies Outlive Their Purpose
text:
Institutions are usually created to solve a specific problem, and they are rarely dissolved when the problem is gone. A wartime agency survives the war. A committee formed for one crisis quietly reappears in the budget for the next twenty years.

The mechanism is not sinister, which is precisely why it is difficult to fight. The people inside an organisation are not conspiring to keep it alive; they simply have expertise, relationships, and mortgages tied to its continued existence. Meanwhile nobody outside has a strong enough incentive to spend political capital on closing something that costs relatively little.

The cost, however, is not primarily financial. It is attention. Every surviving structure occupies space in the schedule of decision makers and consumes the scarcest public resource: the ability to notice new problems. Organisations that cannot die crowd out the ones that should be born.

title: The Second-Language Self
text:
Researchers studying bilingual speakers have repeatedly found something strange: people make more rational decisions when they reason in a foreign language. Presented with the same dilemma, participants show less loss aversion and fewer moral inconsistencies in their second language than in their native one.

The leading explanation is emotional distance. Words learned in childhood arrive with a full load of associations, memories, and social conditioning. Words learned in a classroom at twenty five arrive lighter. The foreign language creates a small gap between the thought and the reflex, and in that gap deliberation happens.

This has an uncomfortable corollary for anyone learning a language. Fluency is not just a set of skills you add to yourself; it slowly builds a slightly different self, one that argues, jokes and even lies in a different register. Advanced learners often describe the moment they first noticed it as unsettling rather than triumphant.
